01Why now

Why this course, and why now

Most people learn architecture by absorbing it from the one or two systems they have worked on. This level gives you the shared vocabulary and the working method first: requirements and constraints, structure, patterns, views, evaluation, and how to decide when and how to use AI. It follows the topics of the iSAQB Foundation Level curriculum, so it is also a way to prepare for that exam.

02Outcomes

What you will be able to do

Speak the language

Use the core terms of architecture correctly: structure, building blocks, views, quality, decisions and the architect’s role.

Find what shapes the design

Separate architecturally significant requirements from the rest, and capture stakeholders, constraints and quality goals.

Design and describe

Work top-down and iteratively, choose patterns with reasons, and describe the result in views others can read.

Evaluate and be exam-ready

Review a design against its goals, judge the use of AI in architecture work, and take a timed mock exam with a gap list.

03Syllabus

20 lessons in 6 modules

Module 1What architecture is

Terms, roles and where architecture sits in a team.

  1. What software architecture is and why it matters
  2. The architect’s role and the people around it
  3. Architecture, design and code: where one ends and the next begins

Module 2Requirements and constraints

What shapes the design before you draw anything.

  1. Stakeholders and their concerns
  2. Architecturally significant requirements and quality goals
  3. Constraints and influencing factors

Module 3Designing the solution

Structure, principles, patterns and technology choices.

  1. Top-down and iterative design
  2. Design principles: abstraction, information hiding, coupling and cohesion
  3. Architectural and design patterns, and choosing technology
  4. Interfaces and cross-cutting concepts

Module 4Specifying and communicating

Views and documentation people will actually read.

  1. Views and viewpoints: context, building blocks, runtime, deployment
  2. Documenting with arc42, a first look
  3. Recording decisions
  4. Diagrams that communicate

Module 5Evaluating, risk and AI

Test a design, name its risks and decide how to use AI.

  1. Evaluating an architecture: scenarios and reviews
  2. Risks and technical debt
  3. Deciding on AI in architecture work and verifying what it produces

Module 6Exam readiness

For the iSAQB CPSA-F exam. Also useful as a check of your own understanding.

  1. How the multiple-choice exam works
  2. Reading questions: recall, understand and apply
  3. A timed mock exam, your gap list and an exam-day plan

This level follows the topics of the iSAQB CPSA-F curriculum (version 2025.1). It is Intellica self-study, not an iSAQB course, and Intellica is not an accredited training provider. The exam is booked separately with an iSAQB certification body; training is not required to sit it. Check the current exam format with the certification body before you book.

04The lab

Your architecture file for one system

Pick a system you know. Across the lessons you build one short architecture file for it, then use the same file to prepare for the exam. One project, built in steps after each lesson. Each step has instructions, a finished example, a health check, and saves on your device.

The steps

  1. Name the system, its purpose and its stakeholders
  2. List five architecturally significant requirements with quality scenarios
  3. Record constraints and influencing factors
  4. Sketch context and building blocks, top-down
  5. Choose a pattern and write down why
  6. Write a runtime scenario and a deployment sketch
  7. Review the design against your scenarios and list the risks
  8. Take a timed mock exam, score it and write your gap list

What the health check looks for

  • Every requirement is tied to a stakeholder
  • Every quality goal has a scenario you could test
  • Every pattern choice has a stated reason
  • Every risk has an owner and a next step

The same method as every Intellica course

See it done

Every lesson starts with a finished example, so you know what good looks like.

Do it yourself

Early steps are mostly filled in. Later steps give you a template, then a blank page.

Check your work

Questions bring back what you learned on a schedule, and a health check confirms your lab work is complete and free of placeholders.

Stay current

Courses are built from current research, with sources you can open, and revised when the evidence changes.

The method follows published research on retrieval practice, worked examples and spaced review. Read the evidence and sources.

Intellica certificates show that you finished this course, as reported by your own browser and checked against the course's completion rules.
